issues.legal_issue: The threshold for summoning a person who is not already an accused to stand trial with the accused on the basis of evidence recorded during trial is higher than a prima facie case but lower than satisfaction that the evidence would establish guilt if unrebutted.
material_facts: During the trial, the prosecution sought to summon additional persons on the basis of the complainant’s testimony.
The complainant attributed specific roles to the proposed additional accused and said they were present during and participated in the attack.
issues.conclusion: The power to summon an additional accused requires strong and cogent evidence, more than mere probability of complicity or the prima facie standard used at the framing-of-charge stage, but does not require satisfaction that the evidence would lead to conviction if unrebutted.
issues.legal_principle: Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure permits a court to proceed against a person who is not already an accused if the evidence indicates that the person committed an offence for which they could be tried with the accused. Under Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab, including its discussion of Vikas v. State of Rajasthan, this discretionary and extraordinary power must be exercised sparingly on strong and cogent evidence. The evidence need not establish guilt to the point that it would result in conviction if unrebutted, and the court must not form an opinion on guilt when applying this threshold.

predicates.additional_accused_application_during_tr: The prosecution applied during a criminal trial to have a person not already charged proceed to trial with the accused.
predicates.witness_attributed_specific_roles: A witness gave testimony attributing specific roles in the alleged offence to the proposed additional accused.
predicates.additional_person_may_be_summoned_on_str: A proposed additional accused may be summoned when the evidence is strong and cogent, exceeds the prima facie standard used at the framing-of-charge stage, and does not have to establish that conviction would follow if it went unrebutted.

issues.definition: When an application to add an accused is made during trial and a witness attributes specific roles to the proposed additional accused, the output is that summoning is permitted only on strong and cogent evidence above the ordinary prima facie threshold, without requiring evidence sufficient for conviction if unrebutted.

issues.legal_issue: An order rejecting an application to summon additional accused must be reconsidered when the courts assessed the evidence as though an infallible case or proof beyond reasonable doubt were required.
material_facts: The complainant testified at trial that the proposed additional accused were present and assigned specific roles to them in the attack.
The trial court and the High Court rejected the application after considering inconsistencies and whether the proposed accused could be shown to have committed the offence beyond reasonable doubt.
A later application to summon the proposed additional accused was rejected essentially by reference to the earlier orders.
issues.conclusion: The impugned orders were set aside and the prosecution’s applications were restored for fresh consideration under the correct standard; the Court expressed no view on the merits or guilt of the proposed additional accused.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as explained in Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab, the court must assess whether the evidence is stronger than a prima facie case but must not demand proof beyond reasonable doubt or decide whether the proposed accused would ultimately be convicted. The power remains discretionary and requires strong and cogent evidence; the evidence and application must be reconsidered under that standard without treating the Court’s observations as a determination of guilt.
